s: The sponsor expects a pilot release in March based on a conversation with the CEO. The approved schedule shows April. Neither date has been formally challenged. What should the project manager do FIRST?
o: Quietly plan for March by adding buffer work to the April schedule
Ask the team to start overtime now to keep the March option open
Remind the sponsor that the approved schedule says April and proceed
Find the source of the March date and reconcile it with baseline
e: Find the source of the misaligned expectation and reconcile it with the baseline. Quoting the baseline alone dismisses the sponsor, and overtime pre-commits cost without a decision.

s: Two key stakeholders each believe the product will support their own department's workflow best, and each has been told 'yes' by different team members. The workflows are incompatible. What is the BEST action?
o: Build first for the department that holds more budget influence
Build both workflows in parallel and let each department choose
Convene both with the product owner and decide on business value
Tell each department the other's workflow is out of scope for now
e: Align expectations by making the conflict explicit and deciding on shared value. Building both or favouring power wastes money or erodes trust.

s: A customer representative approves each demo but tells your account manager privately that the product is not what they hoped. What should the project manager do?
o: Meet the representative to explore the gap, then adjust via governance
Schedule extra demos to gather more detailed written feedback from them
Rely on the formal approvals and log the private remarks as informal
Ask the account manager to resolve it directly with the representative
e: Formal approval is not the same as aligned expectations. Explore the gap directly and handle any change through governance.

s: Which technique BEST helps check that stakeholders understand what a deliverable will do before it is built?
o: A longer written requirements document
A prototype or wireframe walkthrough
A risk probability and impact review
An earned value report by work package
e: Prototypes make expectations concrete and reveal gaps early.

s: At a status meeting the customer says the project is 'obviously late', though it is on schedule against the baseline. Their dates came from a sales presentation. What do you do?
o: Re-plan to the customer's dates to restore confidence quickly
Show the baseline and approvals, then close the discussion
Ask the sales team to apologise to the customer at the next meeting
Acknowledge the view, show the baseline, and trace the sales dates
e: Manage expectations by listening, clarifying the baseline and correcting the source of the misunderstanding.

s: A new project has a charter, but team members describe different goals. Two weeks in, designs are diverging. What is the BEST step?
o: Wait another sprint to see whether the designs converge naturally
Reissue the charter to everyone and ask them to confirm they read it
Run a short workshop linking the business case to a shared goal
Assign each person a detailed task list traced to the charter
e: Shared understanding is created by working it through together, not by redistributing a document.

s: The vision for a hybrid product was agreed with the sponsor, but the agile team feels the predictive milestones contradict it. What should you do?
o: Drop the milestones so the agile team can plan to the vision
Facilitate a talk among both streams and the sponsor to reconcile
Escalate the conflict to the PMO for a ruling on which method wins
Instruct the agile team to follow the approved milestones fully
e: Reconcile the vision and the plan together. Drop or enforce without discussion creates resentment.

s: Which artifact BEST expresses a product's vision for an agile team?
o: A backlog ordered by estimated effort and technical risk
The team charter that lists working agreements and roles
A release burndown chart showing remaining story points
A vision statement or roadmap goal tied to product value
e: A product vision and roadmap goal gives the team a shared direction.

s: A subject-matter expert who has been on the project from the start will retire in three months. They are reluctant to document. What is the MOST effective approach?
o: Pair them with a successor and record walkthroughs
Move them off critical tasks now so others learn by doing
Order them to write up everything before they leave
Hire a consultant to reverse-engineer what they know
e: Tacit knowledge transfers best through pairing and conversation, with respect for the expert.

s: New team members take two months to be productive because key decisions are scattered across emails and chats. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Add longer onboarding meetings led by the senior engineers
Switch to a new chat tool with better thread search
Keep one searchable decision log and onboarding guide
Rotate people between projects less often to keep knowledge
e: Make knowledge findable and keep it current with the team's ownership.

s: A vendor's staff hold all knowledge of an interface and the contract ends in four weeks. What should you do?
o: Wait for the contract to end, then hire the vendor back as needed
Start knowledge transfer now and check the transition terms
Extend the contract for another year to keep the knowledge
Have your team rewrite the interface from scratch before it ends
e: Plan the transition early and use the contract's terms. Extending or waiting delays the problem rather than solving it.

s: A stakeholder group in another country says the project's updates are confusing because of idioms and jargon. What should you do?
o: Send updates only in the group's language through translators
Ask the group to read updates more slowly with a dictionary
Use plain language and a glossary, and check understanding
Replace the written text with charts and diagrams alone
e: Effective communication takes the receiver into account. Adapt style and confirm understanding.

s: A team member says they are overwhelmed by notifications from the project channel. What is the BEST response?
o: Ask the member to mute the channel and rely on a weekly summary
Require acknowledgement of each message to prove it was read
Move all project communication to a single email thread
Agree norms for which channel serves what and when to notify
e: Team communication norms reduce noise without losing critical information.

s: Which is the MOST effective way to communicate a complex, sensitive change to an impacted group?
o: A live conversation followed by written confirmation
A detailed document posted to the shared drive
A short chat message with a link to the full details
A mass email sent to everyone with all key points
e: Sensitive or complex messages are best delivered interactively and confirmed in writing.

s: Your dashboard shows 90% of tasks complete but the sponsor asks why customer acceptance is behind. Tasks are counted whether or not they pass review. What is the issue and the BEST fix?
o: Report progress weekly instead of monthly to catch lag sooner
The dashboard is accurate and acceptance delays are a separate issue
It counts activity; track accepted work against done criteria
Add more granular tasks so the percentage moves more smoothly
e: Progress should reflect completed, accepted work. Counting started or unreviewed tasks overstates status; reporting more often or splitting tasks does not fix the measure.

s: A project's SPI is 0.95 for three months and the team says the delay is on a task with plenty of float. How should the project manager interpret this?
o: Do not worry, since an SPI near 1 means the project is on track
Check whether the late task is on the critical path
Re-baseline the schedule now to reflect the current pace
Add resources across all tasks to bring SPI back to 1.0
e: SPI is an overall measure. Verify impact on the critical path with schedule analysis.

s: In a kanban system, work in progress has grown from 8 to 20 items while throughput is flat. What does this suggest?
o: Cycle time is shortening because the team is working faster
Add team members to raise throughput and clear the work
Flow is slowing: apply WIP limits and find the bottleneck
Pull more work onto the board so nobody sits idle
e: Rising WIP with flat throughput means longer cycle times. Limit WIP and address bottlenecks.

s: Which is the BEST leading indicator that a release date is at risk in an agile project?
o: Burn-up showing scope outpacing completed work
Total hours logged by the team over the last month
Number of stakeholder meetings held in the iteration
Team satisfaction score from last month's survey
e: A burn-up that shows scope outrunning completion predicts a missed date before it happens.

s: A project is terminated early because the business case collapsed. What should the project manager still do?
o: Hand the records to the PMO and release the team without a review
Still close out: record why, capture lessons, finalise contracts
Pause closure until a replacement sponsor can approve the closing steps
Skip lessons learned, finalise contracts, and release the team quickly
e: Closure activities apply even when a project is terminated early.

s: At closure, a vendor invoice is disputed and the vendor's work is complete. What should you do?
o: Cancel the contract and withhold payment until the vendor agrees
Pay the invoice in full to close the procurement quickly
Close the project and leave the invoice for finance to chase
Resolve it through the contract's dispute process, then close
e: Procurement closure requires resolving claims through the contract's process.

s: Which closing activity BEST helps future projects?
o: Capture data-backed lessons in a findable shared place
Send the full final report to the sponsor for sign-off only
Release the team before the review to stop costs accruing
Archive the plans and records without further analysis
e: Documented, accessible lessons improve organisational process assets.

s: A project manager plans an integrated approach for a product with a regulatory approval gate and agile feature development. What is the BEST way to combine them?
o: Run agile freely and ask for approval once it is finished
Switch the whole project to a predictive plan to suit the gate
Set the gate as a fixed milestone with compliance in done
Do all compliance work in one phase just before the gate
e: Integrate compliance into iteration outputs while keeping the gate as a fixed milestone.

s: The integrated plan changes after an approved scope change. Which should be updated?
o: Only the risk register, since scope changes alter risk
Only the scope baseline, because the change was to scope
Only the schedule, then wait for the next phase review
All affected baselines and plans, plus the change log
e: Integrated change control keeps the plan set consistent.

s: Your project must decide how to tailor processes for a small, low-risk project in a large organisation with heavy standards. What is the BEST approach?
o: Skip the standards that feel heavy for a small project
Tailor the standards to size and risk, with approval
Let the team choose which standards to follow on its own
Apply every standard in full to stay consistent with others
e: Tailor for fit while respecting organisational governance.

s: After release, usage data shows that a heavily requested feature is rarely used. What should the team do?
o: Add similar features to the backlog to raise engagement
Wait another release to see whether usage picks up
Find out why with the product owner and reprioritise
Treat usage data as unreliable and rely on request volume
e: Value-based delivery uses evidence to change direction.

s: The cost of a planned feature has risen so that its expected return is below the threshold. The feature is 20% complete. What is the BEST approach?
o: Compare remaining cost with remaining value
Cancel it, since the return fell below the threshold
Continue, because 20% of the budget is already spent
Cut quality to hold the cost within the original budget
e: Ignore sunk cost; decide on what remains.

s: Users trained on a new system revert to their old spreadsheets after two weeks. What is the BEST response?
o: Repeat the training for every user with the same content
Mandate use of the new system and disable the spreadsheets
Pause the rollout until users are ready to adopt it
Ask users why, remove barriers, and enlist their managers
e: Sustained change needs barrier removal and reinforcement, not just mandates or more training.

s: A reorganisation will change several roles on your project's customer side. What should you do?
o: Wait until the reorganisation settles before re-engaging them
Assess impact, update the registers, and re-engage new owners
Stop involving that group and let your team decide for them
Escalate to HR and take no project action until it replies
e: Organisational change affects engagement and risk and should be handled actively.

s: An impediment recorded by the team is blocked on an approval that only the CFO can give. The CFO's calendar is full for a month. What should you do?
o: Escalate with quantified impact and options such as a delegate
Wait for the CFO's calendar to clear and review progress then
Work around the approval using budget the team already controls
Approve it yourself in the CFO's absence and inform them afterwards
e: Escalate with impact and options to the right decision maker.

s: Two issues are open: one blocks the critical path and has no workaround; the other annoys a stakeholder but has no schedule impact. How should you prioritise?
o: Neither of them until the next scheduled project review
The stakeholder issue first, because of the person involved
The critical path issue; keep the stakeholder informed
Both equally, splitting the team evenly across them
e: Prioritise by impact on objectives, and communicate on the rest.
